glyph-globe: globe · parallel rays · one point where they run down the radius
glyph-flat: flat map · the same bearings, laid off straight · they miss
reads-running: running — reset returns to the documented instant
reads-hollow: hollow dots cannot, and carry no ray
ecl-eclipse-note: which is what an eclipse is
exp9-none: No station in this list has the {body} above the horizon at this instant. Run the clock on, or reset to the documented instant.
exp9-out: At {label}, the widest disagreement among these stations is at {worstName}: the {body} is {worstBearing}° from true north, and the flat map says {worstFlat}° — a gap of {worstDiff}°. The narrowest is {bestName}, where the gap is only {bestDiff}°{extra}.
exp9-extra: , which a protractor and a string will not resolve
exp9-verd-big: Verdict rule. At {worstC} the two models do not differ in size but in direction: one sends you {v}° round the horizon from the other. Measure the bearing to ±5° and one of them is finished. If it agrees with the flat map, the globe prediction is refuted; if it agrees with the great-circle bearing to the published sub-point, no choice of lamp height rescues the disc, because the disc's bearing has no lamp height in it.
exp9-verd-small: Verdict rule. The largest gap available at this instant is {v}°, at {worstC}. That is measurable with care but not with a phone compass, so use the shadow-and-noon method — or run the clock on, or take the December instant, where the gap passes 90° and the two models point opposite ways round the horizon.
par-none: Fewer than two of these stations have the Moon above the horizon at this instant, so there is no baseline to measure along. Run the clock on, or reset to a documented instant.
par-row-pair-note: the two stations that can both see the Moon and whose sight lines open widest — chosen by that rule, not by hand
par-row-dist-note: great circle, from the published station coordinates
par-row-baseline: Baseline across the line of sight
par-row-baseline-note: the part of the straight line between them lying across the direction of the Moon: b in the formula
par-row-shift: Shift of the Moon against the stars
par-row-shift-note: θ: computed here, measured by nobody — the angle between the two sight lines
par-row-recon-note: b / (R sin θ), and nothing else whatever
par-row-horiz-note: 1 / sin π, with π = {v}′: one published number, the classical form
par-row-ephem-note: Meeus — what the two reconstructions are checked against, not what they are derived from
par-row-sun: The same measurement on the Sun
par-row-sun-note: the widest opening the Sun gives anywhere on this planet: the negative witness
exp9b-none: Fewer than two of these stations can see the Moon at this instant, so this measurement has no baseline. Reset to a documented instant, or run the clock on until two of them can.
exp9b-out: At {label}, {An} and {Bn} lie {km} apart and both have the Moon above the horizon. Between those two viewpoints the Moon stands {th}′ apart against the background stars — {ratio} times its own diameter, so a single photograph from each place settles it. That one angle gives {dR} Earth radii, against {ephemR} from this page's ephemeris, and it needed no distance, no horizon and no clock beyond the agreed instant.
exp9b-sun-note: The same two sight lines to the Sun open by only {v}″, which is why this experiment does not work on the Sun.
exp9b-verd: Verdict rule. The globe fails if your measured shift does not put d/R within your own uncertainty of the almanac's, or if the answer changes when you turn the baseline. The flat model fails on the table above: the kindest of the three lamp heights at this instant is {H} km, and even that one misses some station's altitude by {err}°
exp9b-verd-down: — and at {down} of these {total} places the Moon is below the horizon right now, where a lamp hung over a plane is above it from everywhere, at every height.
